The experiment lives at cdn.jamesst.one, which now serves a copy of this site, and you can watch where it is routing at rum.jamesst.one.

The above diagram is actually a simplification, because before that, a client first has to look up the IP address to connect to, i.e. DNS. A multi-CDN hooks into the DNS reply and picks which CDN is best, then that CDN’s anycast picks which specific data center based on network routing rules.

The CDN is chosen in DNS. When your resolver asks for cdn.jamesst.one, the answer is a CNAME to one of three CDNs, and which one depends on where you are. Or, more accurately, the network you are on.

The first version used a small script on the page that read Resource Timing entries and beaconed them home. It worked, but I would rather not put JS on pages for this. jsDelivr itself gets its RUM data from elsewhere: it used Cedexis, then PerfOps, rather than running a script of its own.

items.title: Let's Play with Hardcaml!
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
I prepared a five-minute lightning talk for the 8th Homebrew CPU Meetup on November 28, 2026. The slides are below.

Open slides in a new tab · Download PDF · View Markdown source

This talk is a gentle introduction to Hardcaml, an RTL design library embedded in OCaml. Rather than discussing advanced verification techniques, I wanted to share the fun of building digital circuits in an interactive programming environment.

We start with a simple 5-bit counter and do everything inside utop, an OCaml REPL:

No FPGA, external Verilog simulator, or even a separate OCaml project is needed to try this example. I tested the installation steps and the REPL session in a Docker environment, so you can follow along with the slides.

With the help of AI coding agents, I ended up building a dual-core RISC-V SoC that boots Linux 6.18 with SMP on a Colorlight i9 FPGA board.

I hope this talk encourages more people to give Hardcaml a try and enjoy building their own digital circuits.

items.title: Silence
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
And then, there is the silence. The silence when you've just finished a book.

It's a weird silence, not a silence as far as sound goes. Roadwork is still roaring by the window, the fan is still humming slowly, the dog is still munching on its kibbles. But a silence of the mind.

The characters have been jumping out the pages and into your mind, each speaking with their own voice, sharing vivid images of their lives. You are somewhere with them, listening to them, and then the last page, you close the book and there's the silence.

A silence of pondering, not really knowing what to say next. The usual voice inside your mind hasn't taken its place back, it's empty and quiet.

You are left with feelings that precede thoughts. Feelings that are part your own, part those of the book. Illusions of your life pasted onto the ones of the characters.

Feelings filled of what ifs and rememberings of what could have been and what could be.

items.title: Every Layer Removes a Reading
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
On 05/11/2026 Datadog's engineering blog published How we continuously validate formal specifications in production. They wrote TLA+ specifications for parts of their event database, then built a tool, FETCh, that turns each specification into a runtime monitor: every action in the specification becomes a function, every production event is matched to an action, and a failed precondition means the system did something the specification forbids. The sentence that matters is this one: "Reviews provide a point-in-time evaluation, while production systems continue to evolve." And the consequence: "Because the specification itself still appears correct, that drift can create a false sense of confidence."

That post is the prompt for this one. A formal specification is a claim about a system. Checking the specification proves something about the specification. Nothing in that loop looks at the system. The Datadog team closed the loop by reading what production actually did. I have spent…

ZFS makes it easy to answer questions like “How much free disk space does this pool have?” The question “What’s using up all my space?” is much harder to answer thanks to snapshots, clones, reservations, volumes, compression, and referenced data. These features might also cause problems when trying to use traditional filesystem management methods on ZFS datasets. It’s even possible to find you don’t have enough space to delete files, which feels nonsensical until you understand why.

I recently caught up with a good friend, who is also an author. We were discussing the topics that had caught our minds recently. I referred to the latest edition of my newsletter . He searched his inbox and, finally, found it in his spam folder which he promptly fished my emails out of.

items.title: 75% of Rockstar’s workers have voted against unionizing
items.label: Hobbies and Creative
items.excerpt:
The IWGB, a union representing some Rockstar workers, has confirmed that workers rejected a deal that would recognize the Rockstar Game Workers Union.

The two-week ballot, which ran from 12 to 26 November, overlapped with the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6. The results were roughly 25% in favor of recognizing the union, and 75% against, with the vast majority of its around 1,600 employees participating.

Recognition would have established a formal framework for workers to negotiate collectively over pay, overtime, bonuses, leave, pensions, and the impact of AI and redundancies.

The result does not prevent Rockstar workers from organizing with the IWGB or exercising their trade union rights, but means management will not be formally committed to regular meetings with union representatives. The union is also able to continue representing individual members.

The IWGB says that this has not dissuaded them, and they will continue to try and “win the trust” of Rockstar employees.

items.title: Toasted coconut on pumpkin pie
items.label: Q&A
items.excerpt:
My family has always served pumpkin pie with whipped cream and toasted coconut. I have never met anyone else who has toasted coconut with their pumpkin pie. Where did they get this from?

Totally standard canned pumpkin, evaporated milk, eggs type pumpkin pie. I have a distinct memory of my grandmother toasting sweetened shredded coconut on a baking sheet in the oven and watching it like a hawk because it burns easily. She's no longer with us so I can't ask her. My dad, her son, has no idea. She was a great baker, but not an experimental one. Child of Polish immigrants, grew up on a farm in Connecticut during the Depression. Primarily a homemaker; later in life worked in a grocery store deli.

Internet searches have been unhelpful because they only bring up pie that uses coconut milk or oil as a dairy alternative.

Any ideas? Anyone else with this tradition? Any other interesting pumpkin pie toppings?

items.label: Showcase
items.excerpt:
I just started a new blog where I can post about the process of developing software and tech in general. My first proper article is Runtime Quality Requires Humans which is about the limitations of trying to use AI coding with complex systems. I built a new site because I was tired of dealing with ads and paywalls on sites like Medium.

This was also an experiment in using the Astro web framework to make a complex static site, which worked out really well. I wrote all of the article myself but around half of the website tech was written by Claude Code, which I talk about on the About page. If anyone has feedback or a question, I'd love to hear it here!

items.title: Feed the Scorchpot [$14.99] [Strategy] [Windows] [macOS]
items.label: Gaming
items.excerpt:
You struck a deal with a dragon: twenty years of protection for twenty years of dinner service. The island thrives under the beast's watchful eye, as long as the meals keep coming.

Every year, the dragon wakes up hungrier. You roll dice to work your island, harvest ingredients, fuse them into recipes, and cook them down in the Scorchpot — the pot you keep full or end up in. Get the meal right and you prosper. Get it wrong and you're smoke.

Build farmsteads, shrines, and harbors across your hex-grid island, each one changing how the board pays out. The best runs start with a handful of tiles and end with a machine that buries the dragon in food. Then the odds tighten, the dragon turns picky, and you tear the whole thing down and rebuild while it's on fire.

Feed the Scorchpot, keep the dragon happy, and outlast the contract.

Cook cleverly, plan badly, or just roll with it — the dragon doesn't care how you win, only that you feed the beast on time. And yes, you can pet the…

items.label: Gaming
items.excerpt:
Juice is everything. There is nothing in the Fog. There is no greater honor than to serve the Juice Queen, and the sky is definitely not made of plywood.

Juice Galaxy is a happy place to fly around and smack things and drink juice. And explore things. And just, flip around doing stuff. Use any of a multitude of weapons to clobber and devour the local wildlife. Gather juice to increase your power and take on more powerful enemies.The game is still in active development. There's still a ton of work to do. I want to polish the physics and add a ton more abilities, places, music, items, monsters, and story.Enjoy, and please feel free to leave feedback or suggestions.
